related-article.article-title: Asthma reconsidered: a cumulative data perspective on airway smooth muscle

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Airway smooth muscle (ASM) cells are central to bronchoconstriction and airway hyperresponsiveness in asthma, yet a comprehensive view of their transcriptional landscape has been lacking.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We performed a meta-analysis of publicly available transcriptomic datasets comparing ASM cells isolated from individuals with asthma with those from healthy controls. We included studies that met predefined inclusion criteria, comprising primary human ASM cells isolated from 26 asthma and 32 healthy control subjects. Each dataset was analysed separately, followed by meta-analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Heterogenicity assessment, pathway enrichment and single-sample gene set enrichment analysis were performed. DEGs were further matched with genome-wide association studies (GWASs) of asthma.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: This study identified 150 genes that were consistently dysregulated in asthma-derived ASM cells, compared with those from healthy controls. NLRP2 showed the greatest upregulation in asthma as measured by pooled log2 fold change (effect size) in asthma, whereas ABI3 was the most downregulated. Pathway analysis highlighted prominent perturbation of interleukin (IL)-4 and IL-13 signalling. 13 DEGs overlapped with loci reported earlier in a GWAS asthma database, which further underscores our findings.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first meta-analysis of ASM transcriptomes to delineate a core set of genes and pathways underlying asthma-related airway remodelling. These findings refine our understanding of ASM-specific molecular networks and may guide targeted therapeutics for asthma in future.

p.bold: Meta-analysis of human airway smooth muscle (ASM) transcriptomes identified 150 consistently dysregulated genes in asthma, highlighting IL-4/IL-13 signalling and GWAS-linked loci, defining core ASM molecular pathways driving asthma airway remodelling

institution-wrap.institution: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Asthma is a chronic, heterogeneous respiratory disease affecting >300 million people worldwide, including about 25 million people in the USA [1, 2]. Although the causes and the nature of immune response in the lungs during asthma vary widely among individuals, common symptoms include coughing, chest tightness and bronchoconstriction [3]. Airway remodelling is a pathological characteristic of asthma, marked by chronic structural alterations of the airways with smooth muscle hyperplasia; subepithelial collagen deposition; compromised epithelial barrier integrity with goblet cell metaplasia, resulting in excessive mucus production; and immune cell recruitment [4]. Airway remodelling further worsens airway hyperresponsiveness (an irreversible airway narrowing) by altering airway wall mechanics, and creates airflow obstruction. Airway smooth muscle (ASM) cells play a critical role in structural changes that drive bronchoconstriction and airway dysfunction in asthma [5].

Contractile agonists act primarily through several G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) on the cell surface, initiating a signalling cascade involving G proteins, phospholipase C and protein kinase C. This pathway regulates intracellular calcium release, leading to myosin light-chain kinase phosphorylation and ASM contraction [6, 7]. Glucocorticoids and β2 agonists have long been considered the most effective therapies for treating asthma symptoms by inhibiting the infiltration of immune cells in the airway and promoting bronchorelaxation [8]. However, due to disease heterogenicity and incomplete treatment with steroids, some asthma patients develop resistance to standard treatment, necessitating new strategies to mitigate asthma [9].

Gaining a deeper understanding of the physiological mechanisms governing ASM cell function could improve the identification and optimisation of treatments for individuals with asthma. Alexandrova et al. [10] used cap analysis of gene expression to profile the transcriptomes of bronchial smooth muscle cells from asthmatic and non-asthmatic donors, identifying roughly 600 differentially expressed mRNAs along with significant alteration in 245 intercellular pathways. In a separate study, transcriptomic analysis of glucocorticoid-treated human ASM cells isolated from patients with severe asthma revealed a distinct signature of glucocorticoid-responsive genes, including FKBP5, GLUL, PER1, TSC22D3, CRISPLD2 and KLF15, which aligns with previous findings [11]. Interleukin (IL)-17A, a cytokine mainly produced by the Th17 subset of T cells, promotes airway inflammation by inducing secretion of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8 and tumour necrosis factor-α, along with chemokines from airway epithelial cells, alveolar macrophages, fibroblast, endothelial cells and ASM cells [12]. Transcriptional analysis of IL-17A-stimulated ASM cells obtained from individuals with mild asthma demonstrated upregulation of primary response genes such as IL-6 and CXCL10, along with phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase and p70S6K and activation of multiple NF-κB-dependent genes [13].

A meta-analysis of airway epithelial cell datasets has identified 431 genes differentially expressed in asthma compared with healthy controls [14]. While numerous transcriptomics datasets exist for airway epithelium, only a limited number focus on human ASM. The inherent heterogenicity of asthma and its treatment regimens adds further complexity to pinpointing signature genes in ASM. In the present study, we conducted a meta-analysis of available transcriptomics datasets of human ASM in asthma to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across studies. This approach revealed 150 such genes, and pathway enrichment analysis highlighted the biological pathways most affected. We further validated these candidate genes by comparing them with available genome-wide association study (GWAS) datasets for asthma.

sec.title: Study identification
sec.p: The National Centre for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and the European Molecular Biology Laboratory European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) database were searched using the keywords “asthma” and “airway smooth muscle”. 16 human RNA sequencing studies were identified initially. Datasets with overlapping study populations were removed to avoid duplication. Most studies used cultured ASM cells that were isolated from patients and healthy subjects, but a few analysed endobronchial biopsy samples. To maintain data homogeneity, studies based on endobronchial biopsies were excluded due to low read counts, and two microarray datasets were excluded because of limited gene coverage. After these refinements, raw RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) count data for asthma and healthy control samples were obtained from four publicly available GEO datasets (GSE119578, GSE119579, GSE58434 and GSE94335). These four studies comprised 26 asthma samples and 32 healthy controls (table 1). Most participants were Caucasian; healthy subjects were age-matched and had no smoking history.

sec.title: Differential expression analysis
sec.p: Gene-level raw counts for each study were imported into R and analysed using the DESeq2 package (v.1.38.3) [15]. Sample metadata were carefully curated to match the count matrix columns and ensure accurate annotation. Each dataset was processed independently by creating a DESeqDataSet object and running the DESeq2 pipeline, using the Wald test with “poscount” size-factor estimation to accommodate zero-inflated data, as recommended by GEO2R. Genes with low counts (row sums ≤10) were filtered out. Differential expression was assessed for “Asthma” versus “Control”, generating log2 fold change (log2FC), nominal p-values and Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted p-values with false discovery rate (FDR) <0.1 [16].

sec.title: Meta-analysis and heterogeneity assessment
sec.p: A cross-study meta-analysis was performed with the metaRNASeq package [17]. To assess reproducible evidence of differential expression across studies, study-specific adjusted p-values were combined using Fisher's method [18]. Study-specific log2 fold changes (βᵢ) and their standard errors (seᵢ) were combined using a random-effects meta-analysis to obtain a pooled effect size, random-effect beta (βRE) [18, 19]. Between-study variance (τ2) was estimated by restricted maximum likelihood [20, 21], and inverse-variance weights were defined as wᵢ=1/(seᵢ2+τ2) [19]. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q statistic [22], and quantified with I2, representing the proportion of total variability attributable to between-study heterogeneity rather than sampling error [22, 23]. Genes were initially selected based on Fisher p-values <0.1, together with a minimum |βRE|≥0.5 and directional concordance of 1, defined as consistent upregulation or downregulation across all studies. This permissive thresholding strategy was chosen to maximise sensitivity while ensuring biological coherence across datasets.

Given the limited number of datasets (k=4) and the known conservativeness of random-effects models in small-k settings, Fisher-based results were used to define the primary discovery set, while random-effects and heterogeneity metrics were reported to identify the most stable, high-confidence genes. This integrated framework enables transparent evaluation of reproducibility, effect-size stability and heterogeneity in ASM transcriptomic meta-analysis.

sec.title: Gene annotation
sec.p: Gene-level annotation was performed using biomaRt (Ensembl release for Homo sapiens) [24]. Entrez Gene IDs from the DESeq2 results were mapped to Ensembl Gene IDs and official gene symbols. Only uniquely mapped, valid gene symbols were retained for downstream enrichment analysis.

sec.title: Pathway enrichment analysis
sec.p: Significantly dysregulated genes (FDR<0.1 and |βRE|≥0.5) were analysed for functional enrichment analysis. Entrez IDs were obtained using clusterProfiler (v.4.8.1) and org.Hs.eg.db (DOI: 10.18129/B9.bioc.org.Hs.eg.db) [25]. Reactome pathway analysis was performed with the enrichPathway() function in the ReactomePA R package. Gene set enrichment plots and CNET plots were generated with the enrichplot package [26] and the DOSE package [27], incorporating mapped fold changes and gene symbols.

sec.title: Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis
sec.p: Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) was used to quantify pathway-level activity in individual samples. Normalised gene expression values were ranked within each sample, and enrichment scores were calculated for curated Reactome gene sets by comparing the empirical cumulative distributions of pathway genes against all other genes, yielding a continuous activity score per pathway per sample. Differential pathway activity between disease and control groups was assessed by comparing ssGSEA scores across conditions, with effect sizes estimated using Cohen's d. Statistical significance was evaluated at the pathway level with multiple-testing correction using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR, and pathways with FDR<0.05 were considered significant [28]. This approach captures coordinated transcriptional changes at the pathway level and is robust to interstudy variability.

sec.title: Data visualisation
sec.p: Variance-stabilised transformed expression data from DESeq2 were analysed and visualised using multiple approaches in R (v. 4.2.3). Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed with plotPCA, colouring samples by condition and study. Volcano plots were generated in ggplot2 with ggrepel to highlight the most upregulated and downregulated genes [29], while heatmap, created with pheatmap, displayed selected DEGs from the meta-analysis using z-score normalisation and annotations for condition and study. Violin plots for selected GWAS-relevant genes were produced using ggplot2 and tidyverse, showing expression distributions with embedded box plots for each condition [30, 31]. Finally, protein–protein interaction networks were constructed using the STRING database to illustrate potential functional relationships among significant DEGs [32].

sec.title: Meta-analysis
sec.p: To examine global transcriptional differences in ASM cells from individuals with asthma, we first performed PCA across the RNA-seq datasets. The PCA plot showed no clear clustering or separation between those with asthma and healthy subjects, indicating broadly similar overall gene-expression profiles (supplementary figure S1). This lack of separation may reflect substantial biological heterogeneity, subtle transcriptomic differences not captured by the first two principal components or technical variation among studies. These findings highlight the complexity of transcriptional regulation in ASM cells in the context of asthma.

Given the absence of distinct global patterns, we next identified DEGs within each study and conducted a cross-study meta-analysis. This approach yielded 150 DEGs with q-values <0.1 after correcting for FDR using the Benjamini–Hochberg approach (figure 1a, supplementary table S1), of which approximately 105 genes were upregulated in asthma patients. Considering βRE values, which represent the pooled log2 fold change (effect size), NLRP2, SORBS2 and CCDC88C were the most upregulated genes in asthma, while ABI3, CSF3R and MYH11 were the most downregulated (table 2). A volcano plot depicting all significantly upregulated and downregulated genes, with the top 20 DEGs highlighted, is shown in figure 1a. In terms of statistical significance, NLRP2 (upregulated) and ABI3 (downregulated) were the most extreme genes. Notably, NLRP2 emerged as a strongly upregulated gene in ASM cells from asthma patients, a finding not reported in prior studies. Classic ASM-related genes such as MYH11, COL21A1, IL-1A, IL-1B and IL13RA2, previously implicated in asthma, were also captured by the meta-analysis. The heat map in figure 1b further highlights the top 10 upregulated and 10 downregulated genes identified in the meta-analysis.

Red (upregulated) and blue (downregulated) coloured dots represent differentially (adjusted p-value <0.1) expressed genes (random-effects beta (|βRE|) ≥0.5). The top 20 DEGs are labelled in the plot. b) Consistency of differential expression for DEGs with large effect size. The top 20 DEGs with adjusted p-values <0.1 and pooled effect size |βRE|≥0.5 are shown as a heat map.

sec.title: Heterogenicity profile across the datasets
sec.p: Across all analysed genes, between-study heterogeneity was highly variable (figure 2a). Most genes showed little to no heterogeneity (I2≈0%), while a substantial subset exhibited moderate to high heterogeneity, with I2 values extending beyond 75%. This indicates that, although many effects were consistent across studies, heterogeneity was non-negligible for a proportion of genes.

caption.p: Determination of heterogeneity across genes in the meta-analysis. a) The histogram shows the number of genes at different levels of between-study heterogeneity (I2=0). b) Bubble plot of random-effects meta-analysis effect sizes (βRE) against heterogeneity (I2) for Fisher-significant, directionally concordant genes. Heterogeneity assessment of gene-level effects in a random-effects meta-analysis across datasets. c) The Cochran's Q statistic (QE)–I2 scatter plot shows that, among Fisher-significant and directionally concordant genes, heterogeneity varies widely in magnitude. Each point represents a gene, plotted by QE and the corresponding between-study heterogeneity. Points are coloured by effect direction based on the random-effects meta-analysis estimate (|βRE|≥0.5). Dashed lines mark I2 thresholds for low (25%), moderate (50%) and high (75%) heterogeneity. Labelled genes highlight notable signals.

sec.p: The meta-analysis bubble plot (figure 2b) summarises random-effects estimates (βRE) in relation to heterogeneity (I2). Genes with increased expression (βRE>0.5) are shown in red, and those with decreased expression (βRE < −0.5) are shown in blue, with bubble size reflecting statistical significance (−log10 adjusted p-value). Several genes demonstrated strong and significant effects with high heterogeneity, including CCDC88C, SORBS2, ERVW-1 and NLRP2 among upregulated genes, and MYH11, ACTG2 and CSF3R among downregulated genes. In contrast, some genes with consistent effects across studies displayed low heterogeneity (I2<25%).

The relationship between Cochran's Q statistic (QE) and I2 is presented in figure 2c. Larger QE suggests stronger evidence that studies differ more than expected, while I2 values show the magnitude of heterogeneity. Several genes exhibit high I2 despite consistent directionality, indicating reproducible differential expression with variable effect sizes across cohorts rather than inconsistent signals.

sec.title: Interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling pathway is most dysregulated in ASM from people with asthma
sec.p: To identify the pathways most affected in ASM from people with asthma, we performed Reactome enrichment analysis on DEGs identified in the meta-analysis. Pathway-level analysis of asthma versus healthy controls identified three significantly enriched Reactome pathways, namely IL-4 and IL-13 signalling, GPCR ligand binding and extracellular matrix (ECM) organisation (figure 3a). Interestingly, gene-level changes contributing to these pathway signals were directionally concordant across all four datasets: genes that were upregulated (or downregulated) showed the same direction of change in each study, supporting the reproducibility of the observed transcriptional shifts. All of the associated genes (IL1B, IL1A, IL13RA2, CCL2, CCL11 and MMP3) in IL-4 and IL-13 signalling pathways are upregulated. In contrast, the GPCR ligand binding and ECM organisation pathways were characterised by internally mixed regulation despite cross-study directional consistency at the gene level. For example, PPY, GNG8, APLN and P2RY14 were consistently downregulated within the GPCR pathway, and COL21A1 and ACTG2 were consistently downregulated within the ECM pathway, whereas other pathway members showed consistent upregulation.

caption.p: Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA)-based Reactome pathway analysis and Gene Ontology (GO) cellular component enrichment of differentially expressed genes (DEGs). a) CNET plot of Reactome pathway enrichment analysis highlighting differentially regulated pathways in airway smooth muscle (ASM). Enriched pathways are shown as large nodes, with connected smaller nodes representing DEGs contributing to each pathway. Node size reflects the number of genes associated with the pathway, and node colour indicates gene fold change. b) Box plots show ssGSEA enrichment scores for selected pathways in control and asthma samples. Each point represents an individual sample. Effect size (Cohen's d) and p-value for differences between groups are indicated within each plot. c) Bubble plot showing GO cellular component enrichment. The x-axis (signal) represents strength of enrichment (signal score, proportional to enrichment significance). The colour of the lines and circles corresponds to the false discovery rate (FDR). Circle size represents the number of genes involved in that GO term.

sec.p: ssGSEA was used to evaluate the pathway-level activity of three identified Reactome pathways. Among these, the IL-4 and IL-13 signalling pathways showed significant upregulation in asthma compared with controls (Cohen's d= −0.65, p=0.012), indicating a moderate effect size (figure 3b). In contrast, ECM organisation and GPCR ligand binding pathways did not reach statistical significance and exhibited small effect sizes (d= −0.26 and −0.28, respectively). These results highlight selective activation of Th2-associated cytokine signalling in asthma at the pathway level.

Moreover, Gene Ontology (GO) cellular component analysis using STRING revealed significant enrichment in the “extracellular region” and “extracellular matrix” categories (FDR<0.05), consistent with ASM involvement in structural and inflammatory responses. In figure 3c, bubble size represents the number of genes annotated to each term, and colour indicates the FDR value. Interestingly, enrichment of the “hippocampal mossy fibre to CA3 synapse” category, while less expected, may reflect the interactions of synapse with ASM in asthma (figure 3c).

sec.title: Integration of transcriptomic and GWAS data reveals asthma-associated gene expression alterations in ASM cells
sec.p: To identify genes with both differential expression and genetic association with asthma, we cross-referenced the top DEGs from our meta-analysis of human ASM cells with asthma-related loci reported in GWASs. This integrative approach uncovered several genes that were both significantly dysregulated and genetically linked to asthma susceptibility. Violin plots illustrating normalised expression levels of these GWAS-associated DEGs in asthmatic versus control samples are shown in figure 4. Notable examples include FBN-2, EBF-2, EGFLAM, NTNG1, EGR2 and SERPINB7. Genes such as FBN-2 and EBF-2, which have known roles in ECM organisation and transcriptional regulation, respectively, point to potential contributions to airway remodelling and inflammation in asthma. These findings strengthen the connection between genetic risk loci and functional transcriptomic changes in ASM, highlighting candidate genes that may drive asthma pathophysiology.

caption.p: Violin plots showing differentially expressed genes that are matched with the genome-wide association study (GWAS) database.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Asthma reflects a complex interplay of immune and structural cells within the lung, giving rise to diverse clinical manifestations. Comorbid conditions such as obesity, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis and food allergy add further layers of complexity, reinforcing the view of asthma as an umbrella term rather than a single disease [33]. Despite wide variation in disease onset, phenotype and immune response, most cases converge on the central features of bronchoconstriction and airway obstruction. ASM cells play a key role in driving airway obstruction through increased mass and proliferation, and produce mediators to amplify inflammatory responses [34, 35]. Identifying global gene-expression changes in ASM is therefore critical for understanding disease mechanisms. In this study, we performed transcriptomic meta-analysis of human ASM cells obtained from asthmatic patients and matched healthy subjects. We identified 150 genes differentially expressed in asthma. Pathway analysis highlighted significant enrichment of the IL-4 and IL-13 signalling, ECM organisation and GPCR ligand-binding pathways, and several dysregulated genes overlapped with asthma-associated loci in the GWAS database, underscoring the relevance of our findings.

Although several meta-analyses of transcriptomic datasets have focused on airway epithelial cells, no prior meta-analysis has specifically examined ASM cells to identify asthma-related DEGs [14, 36], to our knowledge. Of the 16 ASM-related studies in the GEO database, most were derived from endobronchial biopsy samples with low read counts, probably reflecting contamination from other tissue types and, consequently, poor coverage of smooth muscle-specific genes. In addition, several datasets relied on microarray technology and contained limited gene coverage. To ensure consistency and data quality, these studies were excluded from our analysis. Even after accounting for these factors, a moderate level of between-study heterogeneity remained among the included datasets. Although all four datasets were generated under comparable culture conditions, differences in patient age and asthma severity may have contributed to the observed heterogeneity. Moreover, variation in sequencing depth, sample composition and experimental context may have further increased heterogeneity. Our meta-analysis identified 150 DEGs, including several genes that were not detected in any individual study. Notably, NLRP2 emerged as the most strongly upregulated gene in ASM cells in asthma, consistent with previous literature demonstrating that NLRP2 is highly expressed in the airway epithelium during air pollution-induced lung inflammation [37]. By contrast, the NLRP3 inflammasome plays a predominant role in neutrophilic asthma, where it is required for the production of active IL-1β and is elevated in the sputum of patients with severe disease [38]. In a steroid-resistant mouse model infected with chlamydia and haemophilus, enhanced expression of NLRP3, caspase-1 and IL-1β was observed, driving neutrophilic inflammation and airway hyperresponsiveness [39]. Together, these studies underscore the involvement of NLRP3 in asthma pathogenesis. Therefore, the strong upregulation of NLRP2 observed in our analysis may represent a phenomenon specific to ASM cells, suggesting that NLRP2 could serve as a novel, cell type-specific target in asthma pathophysiology.

One of the hallmark Th2 inflammation-associated genes, IL13RA2, was found to be upregulated in our study. IL-13 promotes proliferation and cholinergic-induced contraction of ASM cells and stimulates collagen synthesis by fibroblasts, thereby contributing to airway remodelling and lung fibrosis [40]. The proinflammatory cytokine IL-1β reduces the ability of isoproterenol to relax cultured human ASM cells, dampening responsiveness to β-adrenergic agonists [41]. IL-1β also supports eosinophil survival through the induction of granulocyte−macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), which may increase inflammatory cell accumulation in the airways [42]. Consistent with these observations, our meta-analysis revealed upregulation of both IL-1B and IL-1A in ASM. IL-1β further promotes MMP-12 secretion from ASM cells via ERK, JNK, PI3K and AP-1 signalling pathways, and our results confirm activation of this IL-1β and MMP-12 axis in asthma [43]. ASM cells are known to produce multiple MMPs that cleave ECM components and regulate matrix turnover, remodelling and angiogenesis [44]. Immunostaining studies have demonstrated localisation of MMP-3 in the submucosal matrix of patients with chronic asthma, aligning with our finding of MMP3 upregulation in asthmatic ASM [45]. This observation is further supported by the enrichment of ECM and extracellular region-related components identified in our GO analysis.

Smooth muscle myosin heavy chain 11 (MYH11), which encodes a key contractile protein in ASM, was downregulated in our analysis. This finding supports the concept that ASM cells in asthma may undergo phenotypic switching from a contractile to a synthetic or proliferative state, characterised by reduced expression of contractile proteins such as MYH11 and increased production of ECM components and cytokines [46]. Chronic airway inflammation may drive this structural remodelling, as proinflammatory cytokines suppress MYH11 expression while promoting ASM proliferation and hypertrophy [47]. Another notable gene, collagen type XXI alpha 1 chain (COL21A1), was also downregulated. Type XXI collagen is a fibril-associated collagen with interrupted triple helices (FACIT), and its decreased expression represents a novel finding, contrasting with reports of increased fibrillar collagens in asthma [48]. However, other studies have shown no significant differences in total collagen content between healthy and severely asthmatic lungs [49]. Our results highlight a potential role for altered FACIT collagen expression in asthma pathogenesis. Reduced COL21A1 could impair the structural organisation of collagen fibrils, alter the mechanical properties of the ECM and contribute to dysregulated smooth muscle behaviour. Furthermore, COL21A1 downregulation may increase A SM susceptibility to pro-remodelling signals such as transforming growth factor-β or platelet-derived growth factor, thereby reinforcing a synthetic, ECM-producing phenotype.

ERVW-1 emerged as an intriguing gene in our analysis. Upregulation of human endogenous retrovirus (HERV) genes has been linked to several diseases but has not previously been reported in asthma. A population-based study demonstrated that air pollution can enhance methylation of HERV-K and HERV-R, while reducing methylation of HERV-L and LINE1, in children with asthma living in inner-city environments [50]. In addition, antibodies against the HERV-W envelope protein are elevated in patients with multiple sclerosis and have been proposed as biomarkers of disease progression [51]. Together, these findings raise the possibility that HERV activation in ASM may contribute to inflammation associated with asthma.

The second most upregulated gene in our study, sorbin and SH3 domain containing 2 (SORBS2), has no established link to asthma. However, SORBS2 plays a key role in maintaining structural integrity in cardiomyocytes, suggesting a potential, though as yet untested, connection between cardiac function and asthma-related airway remodelling [52]. Interestingly, several senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) genes encoding cytokines (IL-1A, IL-1B, CCL11 and CCL13) and structural or matrix-associated proteins (MMP3, MMP12, COMP, SPARCL1 and FBN2) were identified in our meta-analysis. Cellular senescence has been increasingly implicated in asthma pathogenesis, where damage-induced senescent airway cells accumulate and adopt a SASP characterised by the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines and matrix-remodelling factors [53]. In addition, SERPINB7, a member of the serpin superfamily, emerged as an important gene in our meta-analysis, while another family member, SERPINB1, has been reported as upregulated in airway epithelial cells [14]. The consistent identification of the SERPINB family gene across meta-analyses of ASM and epithelial cells supports the notion that their function in asthma may be conserved across multiple airway compartments, despite tissue-specific patterns of expression.

CNET plot and pathway enrichment analysis identified IL-4 and IL-13 signalling as a central inflammatory axis in ASM. Enrichment of this pathway, driven by upregulation of IL1A, IL1B and IL13RA2 genes and associated chemokines encoding genes such as CCL2 and CCL11, highlights sustained cytokine responsiveness within ASM that extends beyond its classical contractile function. IL-4 and IL-13 signalling is known to modulate ASM proliferation, calcium mobilisation and contractility, and to promote the release of pro-inflammatory and pro-remodelling mediators.

ECM organisation pathway formed a distinct yet interconnected module characterised by altered expression of structural and remodelling genes (COL5A3, COL21A1, FBN2, COMP, HAPLN1) alongside matrix-degrading enzymes (MMP3, MMP12), reflecting dysregulated matrix turnover and airway remodelling. Differential expression of FBN2 and COL21A1 suggests ECM disorganisation rather than simple matrix accumulation. FBN2 supports elastic microfibril integrity while COL21A1 regulates collagen fibril organisation, collectively pointing to defective collagen assembly and abnormal ECM architecture [54]. Notably, the connectivity observed between IL-4 and IL-13 signalling and ECM organisation genes, including MMP3 and MMP12, suggests a mechanistic link whereby type 2 cytokine-driven ASM activation may directly contribute to airway remodelling through altered matrix turnover. In contrast, the directionally consistent, yet internally mixed, regulation observed within the GPCR ligand-binding and ECM organisation pathways is likely to reflect the complex remodelling and signalling adaptations of ASM, in which specific GPCRs and ECM components are selectively suppressed or activated rather than globally regulated. Such heterogeneous yet reproducible transcriptional changes are consistent with the dynamic balance between contractile function, structural remodelling and inflammatory signalling that characterises chronic asthma pathology.

GO enrichment analysis using the STING platform revealed significant enrichment of cellular components associated with the extracellular region, extracellular space, ECM and cell periphery, pointing to a convergence of upregulated gene activity within these cellular compartments. Another notable finding was the enrichment of the hippocampal mossy fibre to CA3 synapse GO term, which is particularly interesting. Synapse-like molecular machinery has been described in non-neuronal cells, including smooth muscle, where it supports rapid signal integration and contractile responses [55]. Furthermore, 13 genes in our DEG list overlapped with asthma-associated loci identified through GWASs, underscoring the value of this meta-analysis in uncovering genes with potential relevance to asthma pathogenesis.

A key limitation of this meta-analysis is the modest sample size, reflecting the relative scarcity of transcriptomic studies of ASM compared with airway epithelial cells. Although limited covariate data (including age, sex and treatment) were available across datasets, small sample sizes within individual studies precluded statistically robust covariate-adjusted or sex-stratified analyses. Given known sex-dependent differences in ASM biology, such adjustments would be informative; however, incorporating these variables would have resulted in a substantial loss of statistical power and an increased risk of unstable or false-positive estimates. Despite these limitations, the principal strength of this study lies in the integration of multiple RNA-seq datasets through meta-analysis, which increases the effective sample size and enhances the detection of reproducible transcriptional signatures across independent studies. Differential expression analysis was performed separately for each dataset, ensuring appropriate within-study normalisation and statistical inference while minimising biases arising from platform- or study-specific effects. Nevertheless, statistical power within individual analyses may remain limited in smaller cohorts due to biological variability and the absence of covariate adjustment.

The subsequent combination of results using Fisher's method provides an efficient means of aggregating statistical evidence across studies; however, this approach assigns equal weight to all datasets and does not account for differences in sample size or effect-size variance, potentially reducing sensitivity to subtle but consistent effects. The application of stringent significance thresholds (adjusted p<0.1 and |βRE|≥0.5), together with the requirement for consistent effect direction across studies, further enhances specificity, albeit at the expense of reduced power. Overall, our findings provide a framework for understanding signalling networks altered in ASM in asthma and highlight candidate pathways and genes with potential therapeutic relevance. Importantly, this study serves as a foundation for future meta-analyses incorporating larger, better-annotated datasets to validate and extend these observations.
